short: Made sentence lipreading measurable with LRS, but its decoder and curriculum gains are confounded with data and augmentation, and the beats-a-lipreader claim is on unequal terms.
position: The paper [1] changed three components: a dual-attention character decoder (M06), a word-to-sentence length curriculum (M03) and an automatically built BBC sentence benchmark (M11). M11 is its lasting contribution: its pipeline became LRS2-BBC and LRS3-TED [2], although LRS itself was never released [3]. The decoder is standard: LAS carried over from ASR. On LSVSR data a phoneme-CTC system with an external language model later reached 40.9% against 76.8% WER for an attention model [4], but units, front end and decoding differ, so the decoder's share is unknown. The curriculum is standard: its 76.5% to 61.1% WER gain is one run, later attributed to sub-sequence augmentation [5]. "Better than a professional lipreader" holds in direction (50.2% against 73.8% WER), but the conditions are unequal, the machine is not shown to have read the same 200 clips, and speaker independence is asserted, not shown.

verification_status.note: All 8 required evaluator fixes were checked against the source text, the wiki or the publisher record; none remains unverifiable. New numbers (Auto-AVSR 14.6/19.1% WER, LP-Conformer 12.8% WER and 100k hours, VTP 30.92/30.91% WER) need notes.json entries before the gate's number trace passes.
